title: The Proxy Conversation Starts With What Matters
subtitle: Before anyone fills out a form, make space for the older person to say what a good life looks like—and whom they trust to speak for them.
imageAlt: An older woman talking with her adult daughter and son-in-law at a kitchen table, with a notebook open between them.
imageConcept: A warm, natural kitchen-table scene: an older family member leads a conversation with an adult couple who are listening, not taking over. A blank notebook and a cup of tea sit nearby; no medical paperwork or staged expressions of distress.
body:
A conversation about who might speak for someone during a health crisis can sound like a legal errand. It is also a chance to learn what that person wants others to understand about their life. The two purposes belong in that order: listen first, sort out documents later.

The older family member should set the pace and decide whether to take part. An adult child and their partner might ask, “Would you be open to talking about what matters to you if you couldn’t speak for yourself?” If the answer is no, or not today, accept it. Advance-care planning is voluntary; a family discussion is not a decision made on the person’s behalf [1].

Choose a calm, private setting and leave enough time for pauses. This need not be a formal family meeting, and it does not have to resolve every question. The useful first outcome may simply be that everyone understands why the conversation matters and agrees on whether to continue.
Ask what the person wants life to make room for

Begin with ordinary life rather than a list of medical treatments. What helps a day feel worthwhile? Which routines, relationships, abilities, or places matter especially? What would the person want clinicians and family to know about what makes life feel like their own?

These questions invite more than a quick preference. Someone might value being able to recognize and talk with family, while another person may place particular importance on independence, comfort, faith, or time at home. The point is not to rank those values for them. It is to understand what they mean in that person’s words. A conversation guide from the National Institute on Aging recommends discussing values and wishes with the person who may serve as a proxy [1].

Listen for the reasoning as well as the answer. If the person says, “I want to be comfortable,” ask what comfort means to them. If they mention staying at home, ask what they value about being there. Clarifying gently can make a broad statement more useful without turning the exchange into an interrogation.
Choose a listener who can carry the person’s wishes

A health-care proxy is someone chosen to make health-care decisions if the person cannot make or communicate themself. That is different from a living will, which records preferences about treatment. Both are common kinds of advance directives, but they serve different roles [1]. A proxy’s job is not to substitute their own preferences for the person’s; it is to represent the person as faithfully as possible.

Ask whom the person trusts to take on that responsibility. Trust may matter more than family rank, geography, or who is most comfortable speaking in a hospital. The right person is the one the individual chooses, not automatically the oldest child, spouse, or most forceful voice in the room. The person may also want to identify someone else to contact or serve as a backup, if the relevant form allows it.

The adult couple can make room for the choice without lobbying for it. A useful question is, “Is there anyone you would feel comfortable having speak for you—and anyone you would not want in that role?” The answer belongs to the person whose care is at issue.
Help the chosen person understand, not guess

Naming someone is only part of the work. A proxy may later have to make decisions under pressure, with limited information and no opportunity to ask what the person would say. Talking through the person’s values now gives that trusted decision-maker more to work with than a name on a form.

Ask what the chosen person should understand about the older adult’s priorities, worries, and boundaries. Invite examples: What kinds of abilities or daily experiences feel essential? What would the person want the proxy to ask clinicians to explain? Are there family, cultural, spiritual, or personal considerations they want included in care discussions? The person can answer as much or as little as they want; no one needs to force certainty about every possible medical scenario.

The National Institute on Aging advises sharing completed planning documents with the proxy, loved ones, and doctor, and reviewing them when health or life circumstances change [2]. A separate conversation can help the proxy understand the thinking behind the written choices. It is also a chance for the person to correct a misunderstanding before it hardens into family lore.
Keep the conversation open to uncertainty

People do not always know how they would feel in a hypothetical crisis. A family member might hear a clear value in one moment and a different emphasis later, as circumstances or understanding change. That is not a failure to plan. It is a reason to avoid treating one conversation as a permanent verdict.

If an answer is uncertain, write down the question rather than pushing for a yes or no. For example: “Ask the doctor what recovery could realistically involve,” or “I want to understand how this option affects comfort.” The person can bring those questions to a clinician and revisit the discussion afterward. The NIH MedlinePlus planning checklist likewise frames advance-care planning around personal values, discussion with loved ones, and considering who might serve as a proxy [3].

A proxy document and a conversation cannot guarantee a particular outcome. Wishes may be difficult to apply to a situation no one anticipated, and clinicians can help explain medical options. A useful plan leaves room for that reality: it gives the chosen person guidance without pretending that every future decision can be settled in advance.
Move from conversation to the right form

Once the person is ready, the next step is to find the advance-directive form for the state where they live. In the United States, forms and execution rules vary by state; witnessing or notarization requirements may differ too [2]. A family discussion does not appoint a proxy, and a written document should not be assumed valid just because everyone agrees with it.

The person can ask their doctor or another qualified health professional to explain medical questions, and consult a qualified attorney about legal questions or personal circumstances. A living will and a health-care power of attorney are not interchangeable, so check what the state form is designed to do. If the person chooses to complete documents, make sure the selected proxy knows, and ask how copies should be shared with the relevant health-care team.

Keep a note of unresolved questions and who will follow up. The older adult should decide what to document, whom to tell, and where records are kept. The practical aim is not to create a thick file; it is to make the person’s choice and guidance findable when needed.
End with the person’s next question

At the next unhurried family visit, ask the older person whether they would like to continue the conversation. Let them choose one topic: what a trusted proxy should know, which state form to look for, or which medical question needs an explanation. Put that question in their words on a page they control. If they want help, agree who will find the official state information or arrange a clinician conversation, and when to check back. If they would rather pause, leave the page blank. A good handoff is not a completed checklist; it is a next step the person has chosen, with room for their answer to change.
